newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine joblessness falls but rate to stay high.
newsitem.headline: Argentine joblessness falls but rate to stay high.

text.p: Argentina's unemployment rate fell to 16.1 percent in May and official figures showed strong job creation, but analysts said low joblessness could still be years away despite high economic growth.

Unemployment fell from 17.3 percent at the time of the last twice-yearly survey last October, the Economy Ministry announced Friday. The percentage of the population employed or looking for work edged up to 42.1 percent, which economists said showed the creation of 332,000 jobs in six months.
But analysts were not prepared to rejoice.

"These figures confirm the view that you have strong growth, but unemployment falls just one percent each time you measure it," Freddy Thomsen, chief economist at ING Barings Argentina, told Reuters, "It is consistent with the viewpoint that growth by itself is not enough."

Jose Rutman, of Broda y Asociados, agreed that the figures show a painfully slow fall in joblessness. "We could not have hoped for much more," he said. Thomsen argued the government must press ahead with moves to make labor markets and employment contracts more flexible or live with double-digit unemployment for at least two or three years more.
"It provides more ammunition for the supporters of labor reform," he added, "Up to now there have still been some who have thought that maybe we can avoid reform."

The Peronist Party government, facing mid-term congressional elections in October, has bet on returning strong economic growth and a package of labor market reforms to combine to cut unemployment and boost its popularity.
But a government attempt to decree labor laws last year was thrown out by the courts as unconstitutional.

The government then agreed on a less ambitious package of reforms with unions and sent them to Congress for approval, along with a separate set of proposals by employers who want much tougher changes.
Ines Piccinino, economist for Asesores Economicos, welcomed the creation of jobs, but agreed that without labor market reforms joblessness will stay high for some years yet.

"Obviously the tendency is highly positive, with the increase in job creation," she said. "It's still not time to start jumping for joy, but the figures break a tendency, as job creation had been quite slow up to now."
Piccinino added that technological change allowing firms to grow without hiring may also prove a drag on job creation in the absence of sufficient training programs.
Unemployment has ballooned from seven percent when President Carlos Menem took office in 1989 and began a program of economic liberalization which crushed hyperinflation.

Joblessness had risen gradually to 12 percent by the end of 1994, when Argentina was battered by the "Tequila effect" of Mexico's sudden peso devaluation. Unemployment leapt to a peak of 18.4 percent in the resulting deep recession in 1995.
Thomsen said that the labor reforms agreed with the unions would be unlikely to reduce unemployment quickly.
"If you look at key clauses, they come into effect very slowly," he said, stressing that the draft agreement was also quite vague and could easily be modified in Congress.

Discontent led to outbreaks of civil unrest in the poorer provinces in 1995 and has continued sporadically this year. Riots and roadblocks, sometimes set up by thousands of jobless workers at a time, have cropped up from Neuquen in the south up to Jujuy on the border with Bolivia in the north.
